content: Trichotillomania is a condition characterized by hair loss caused by repetitive urges to pull or twist one’s hair until it breaks off. Individuals with this condition are unable to stop the behavior, even as their hair becomes noticeably thinner. The symptoms of trichotillomania often begin before the age of 17. Hair loss may occur in round patches or diffusely across the scalp, resulting in an uneven appearance. In addition to the scalp, individuals may also pull hair from other areas, such as the eyebrows, eyelashes, or other parts of the body. Common symptoms observed in children include an uneven appearance of the hair, bare patches, or widespread hair loss. In some cases, individuals may ingest the hair they pull out, which can lead to bowel obstruction. Other signs include constant tugging, pulling, or twisting of the hair, denial of the behavior, and regrowth of hair that feels like stubble in the affected areas. Additional behaviors, such as other forms of self-injury, may also be present. Furthermore, individuals with trichotillomania often experience associated psychological issues, including feelings of sadness or depression, anxiety, and a poor self-image. Trichotillomania is classified as an impulse control disorder, but its exact causes remain unclear. It is estimated to affect up to 4% of the population, with women being four times more likely to be affected than men. Diagnosis often begins with a visit to a dermatologist, as individuals with trichotillomania frequently seek medical attention for hair loss. A biopsy of the scalp or affected area may be performed to rule out other causes of hair loss, such as infections or other dermatological conditions. Treatment for trichotillomania is multifaceted. While there is no consensus among experts regarding the use of medications, certain drugs, such as naltrexone and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), have shown efficacy in reducing some symptoms. Behavioral therapy, particularly habit reversal training, has also been found to be effective in managing the condition. The prognosis for trichotillomania varies. In younger children, particularly those under the age of six, the condition may resolve on its own without treatment. For most individuals, hair-pulling behavior ceases within a year. However, for others, trichotillomania can become a chronic, lifelong disorder. Treatment often leads to improvements in hair-pulling behavior as well as associated feelings of depression, anxiety, and poor self-esteem. Complications can arise in cases where individuals ingest the hair they pull out, a behavior known as trichophagia. This can result in intestinal blockages or nutritional deficiencies. Prevention of trichotillomania focuses on early detection, as this allows for timely intervention and treatment. Reducing stress levels may also help, as stress is known to exacerbate compulsive behaviors.
